items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Media Organizations: Emerging Practices, Opportunities and Implications for Social and Cultural Development
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly visible part of the modern media environment. Its role is no longer limited to automated or computational journalism; it is now being explored across several stages of media production, including content writing, editing, transcription, translation, fact-checking, audience analysis, recommendation, and personalization. As generative AI and large language models have developed, academic interest in their use within journalism and media organizations has also increased considerably. Recent studies and reviews show that research in this area has expanded from early discussions of automated journalism to broader questions concerning how AI is changing newsroom practices and professional work. This review examines existing research on AI adoption in media organizations, focusing particularly on changes in newsroom practices, organizational processes, journalistic roles, editorial decision-making, and the social and cultural dimensions of AI use. The paper brings together earlier research on automated and algorithmic journalism with more recent literature on generative AI, journalist–AI collaboration, newsroom implementation, ethical concerns, and organizational barriers. The literature suggests that AI can help media organizations handle repetitive and data-intensive tasks more efficiently, allowing journalists to devote greater attention to activities that require interpretation and editorial judgement. However, the growing use of AI also raises important concerns about human oversight, algorithmic transparency, accountability, professional autonomy, and the quality and context of media content. Particular attention is given to India and other countries of the Global South, where the adoption of AI takes place within different economic, organizational, linguistic, and cultural settings. Research from these contexts indicates that AI adoption is developing, but its implementation is not always uniform. Limited resources, inadequate training, organizational preparedness, and the absence of clear ethical guidelines can influence how effectively media organizations integrate AI into their professional practices. Overall, the review suggests that AI adoption in media should not be understood simply as a technological shift aimed at improving speed and efficiency. It is also influencing the nature of journalistic work, editorial responsibility, and the relationship between media organizations and the communities they serve. Therefore, understanding AI adoption requires attention not only to its operational benefits but also to its implications for the social and cultural responsibilities of media.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Copyright: Authorship, Ownership, and Originality
items.abstract: This study critically examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and copyright law by focusing on the three foundational concepts of authorship, ownership, and originality. It evaluates existing legal frameworks, judicial decisions, international developments, and scholarly opinions to determine whether current copyright principles are capable of addressing AI-generated works or whether legislative reform is required, and proposes recommendations aimed at balancing technological advancement with the protection of human creativity.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Quality Assurance: Applications, Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality management by enabling data-driven process monitoring, prediction, automation, and decision support. This narrative review examines the application of AI across major pharmaceutical manufacturing operations and within quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC). The review focuses on machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, predictive analytics, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring, robotics, and digital-twin technologies. Potential applications include raw-material inspection, dispensing and weighing, granulation, blending, tablet compression, capsule filling, coating, packaging, warehouse management, predictive maintenance, documentation review, deviation management, corrective and preventive action (CAPA), validation support, risk assessment, visual inspection, laboratorydata interpretation, stability studies, and process analytical technology (PAT). AI can improve speed, consistency, traceability, and early detection of process or quality problems; however, these benefits depend on data quality, appropriate validation, cybersecurity, system integration, human oversight, and regulatory acceptability. Current regulatory activity, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's discussion paper on AI in drug manufacturing, demonstrates the growing importance of risk-based approaches to AI adoption. Overall, AI should be viewed as an enabling technology that augments, rather than replaces, pharmaceutical professionals. Responsible implementation combining validated digital systems with human expertise may support safer, more efficient, and more reliable pharmaceutical manufacturing.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven reconfiguration of customer experience: A service-dominant logic framework
items.abstract: This study develops a framework explaining how artificial intelligence (AI) reconfigures customer experience in hospitality and tourism, drawing on service-dominant logic. Co-citation and content analyses were conducted to synthesize 89 articles and identify the intellectual structure of the literature. The findings reveal that institutional arrangements condition AI's legitimate participation in service ecosystems. Three mechanisms explain how AI reconfigures customer experience: the actor role architect, the interaction mediator, and the experience orchestrator. These mechanisms operate concurrently and recursively rather than as discrete stages within AI-enabled service ecosystems. The study makes three contributions to the literature. First, it positions customer experience reconfiguration as an ecosystem-level process. Second, it extends service-dominant logic from dyadic to triadic human-AI-human value co-creation. Third, it differentiates AI by functional intelligence, showing that mechanical, thinking, feeling, and multi-functional types perform distinct roles in this reconfiguration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Assessment Integrity, and the Future of Curriculum and Teaching
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) changes the conditions under which universities generate knowledge, organise teaching, evaluate individual achievement and justify academic awards. Its significance is not exhausted by the efficiency of automated tools or the detection of misconduct: AI unsettles the relationship among intended competence, performed intellectual work, submitted evidence and accountable educational judgement. This chapter develops a Rwanda-anchored, critically evidence-based account of responsible AI integration across curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, institutional management and external review. A purposive documentary and conceptual synthesis combines foundational scholarship, recent experimental research syntheses on learning outcomes and assessment validity with UNESCO guidance, the National AI Policy, Rwanda's data-protection law, Higher Education Council instruments and international risk-management benchmarks. It differentiates generative, predictive, adaptive and increasingly agentic applications; examines disciplinary and role-specific AI literacy; and analyses authorship, academic integrity, accessibility, bias, privacy, procurement, academic labour and technological dependence. The chapter's distinctive contribution is an evidence-traceable governance model connecting educational purpose, legitimate authority, bounded AI use, independently interpretable assessment evidence, learner protection and reviewable decisions. Practical instruments include an institutional AI governance and academic assessment integrity framework, task-level disclosure template, assessment-redesign matrix, risk-based tool appraisal and worked hypothetical evaluation. These are original professional proposals, not regulator-approved or independently validated instruments. The chapter concludes that trustworthy AI-enabled higher education requires greater, rather than diminished, human responsibility for what is taught, learned, assessed and certified.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Digital Learning Resilience in Higher Education: An Integrative Review and Capacity-Sensitive Framework for Resource-Constrained Universities
items.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in teaching, assessment and administration in higher education, simultaneously widening educational opportunity and institutional cyber exposure. This review examines how AI-related and conventional cyber threats affect the continuity of digital learning, how AI can both amplify and mitigate those threats, and which integrated responses are feasible for resource-constrained universities, with Nigeria as the illustrative context. Design/Methodology/Approach: A narrative integrative review following established integrative-review guidance synthesised 60 sources published mainly between 2019 and 2026, comprising peer-reviewed studies, technical standards, policy and legal instruments, and institutional or industry reports. Sources were organised by threat mechanism, institutional vulnerability, educational consequence, response and implementation constraint, and each was classified by the type of inference it can support. Findings: Seven overlapping threat clusters were identified: AI-enhanced social engineering and identity abuse; ransomware and extortion; privacy leakage and surveillance; platform and supply-chain compromise; manipulation of AI-enabled learning systems; synthetic media and assessment-integrity attacks; and human, governance and infrastructure weaknesses. Experimental evidence shows that large language models lower the cost of persuasive phishing, while AI-text detectors and automated proctoring raise reliability and fairness concerns. AI-assisted defence offers measurable triage benefits but introduces false alarms, concept drift, privacy exposure and automation bias. Originality/Value: The proposed AI-Cybersecurity-Digital Learning Resilience (AIC-DLR) Framework adapts NIST CSF 2.0 functions to the educational mission, overlays NIST AI risk-management guidance, and treats usable, equitable recovery of teaching and assessment, rather than system restoration alone, as the protected outcome. A tiered roadmap and a set of operationally defined indicators translate the framework into testable practice. Practical Implications: Priorities for low-capacity institutions are accountable ownership, phishing-resistant identity for privileged users, tested and isolated backups, proportionate data practices, governed AI use and pre-authorised alternative learning channels. The framework is conceptual and unvalidated; comparative implementation studies are required to establish its effect on recovery time and equitable access.

items.title: Artificial intelligent in human resources management systems: opportunities, challenges, and implications for modern organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence has moved from the margins of human resource management into its everyday machinery. Applicant tracking systems now rank candidates, chatbots answer policy questions, predictive models flag employees likely to resign, and large language models draft job descriptions and appraisal summaries. Research has grown quickly alongside this adoption, but it remains scattered across human resource management, information systems, operations research and computer science, and the regional scholarship published outside English-language journals is rarely integrated into it. This article reports a systematic review of 82 peer-reviewed studies published between January 2015 and March 2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ScienceDirect and the Russian scientific database eLIBRARY.RU, and screened following PRISMA 2020 guidance. Thematic synthesis produced six themes: recruitment and selection; learning, development and internal mobility; performance management and predictive analytics; employee experience and generative AI; determinants of adoption; and fairness, transparency and governance. Three findings stand out. First, the evidence base is heavily skewed towards recruitment, which accounts for roughly two in five studies, while compensation, industrial relations and occupational safety are barely represented. Second, reported benefits are concentrated in process efficiency, which is comparatively easy to measure, whereas claims about decision quality rest on weaker designs and shorter time horizons. Third, adoption failure is more often organisational than technical: the recurring constraints are data quality, scarce analytical skill inside the HR function, and the absence of an internal governance routine. We argue that value from AI in human resource management depends on treating it as an organisational capability rather than a procurement decision, and we set out a research agenda addressing longitudinal outcome measurement, employee justice perceptions, and evidence from emerging and transition economies. Keywords Artificial intelligence; human resource management; HR information systems; algorithmic decision-making; people analytics; systematic literature review; AI governance; algorithmic fairness

items.title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
items.abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. An interruption budget limits the number of questions, while a user-attention cost charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Beyond question counts, this cost captures perceived effort: on conversation pairs with the same number of questions, human annotators agreed with the cost on which conversation required more effort 75% of the time. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions reduces user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward they earn with unlimited questions. At the same budget, reviewing each question against the memory of users' earlier answers cuts attention cost by another 13% with little reward loss and yields more valuable questions. Models also differ sharply in how well they ask: at the same user-attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others. These results show that asking less and asking better are distinct goals, and that evaluations of proactive agents should measure both.

items.title: Assessing Artificial Intelligence Readiness of Higher Education Institutions in Chhattisgarh: A Study of Faculty and Students
items.abstract: The research measured the readiness of faculty and students of higher education institutions (HEIs) in Chhattisgarh, India in terms of five dimensions: awareness of AI, technical skills, digital infrastructure, policy and institutional support, and attitude toward AI. The data was collected from four types of institutions, through a cross-sectional survey design with the help of stratified sampling technique with 440 respondents consisting of 120 faculty members and 320 students. An overall Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index (ARI) was calculated using a 5-point scale. Readiness was moderate (M = 3.24, SD = 0.45): attitude and awareness and infrastructure and institutional policy were the highest and the lowest scores respectively. Students performed significantly higher than faculty on the ARI, t (205) = 5.41, p < .001, and the readiness differed by institution type, F(3, 436) = 16.0, p < .001, with government colleges being the lowest. The results showed that 62.7% of the variance of attitude towards AI could be accounted for by awareness, skills, infrastructure and policy support. The results highlight an infrastructure-governance gap as a more likely cause than a motivation gap, and suggestions are provided on paths forward for state policymakers and institutional leaders. Note: The data analysed in this draft are illustrative (simulated) and must be replaced by actual survey responses prior to submission and/or publication.

items.title: Assessment of Cognitive Engagement in Virtual Reality Using Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS)
items.abstract: This pilot study investigated prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation during a mental arithmetic task in a virtual reality (VR) environment, using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to assess cognitive engagement. Seven university students completed a relaxation phase followed by a VR-based arithmetic task while brain activity was recorded using a 16-optode continuous-wave fNIRS system. Oxygenation levels were compared between relaxation and task phases across four PFC subregions using paired t-tests. The left dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) showed significantly higher oxygenation during the math task compared to relaxation ( p = .026). Other regions exhibited similar but nonsignificant trends. These patterns are consistent with prior real-world fNIRS studies on mental arithmetic. The findings support the feasibility of combining fNIRS with VR for cognitive engagement research in educational and human factors contexts.

items.title: Assisted Snapshot GNSS Position, Navigation, and Timing for LEO Satellites
items.abstract: This paper presents a novel conceptual design for a low Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) snapshot Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning system for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) CubeSats to enhance their Space Situational Awareness (SSA). Assisted GNSS (aGNSS) strategies allow for small snapshot collections of GNSS signals to be used for full position, velocity, and timing solutions at low-power usage. Key limitations of commercial GNSS receivers for CubeSats and the benefits of aGNSS strategies are discussed. Conceptual designs for the receiver architecture for power-efficient implementation are presented. Computation times and power usage are tested with common microprocessors for major functions and algorithms utilized in the full implementation. Methodologies for initial orbit determination and predictions are discussed to enable computation of aGNSS solutions in a dynamic LEO environment, with examination of the importance of an accurate drag parameter and fit span considerations. Strategies that allow efficient updates to GNSS ephemerides by utilizing a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) GNSS receiver are explored. Tests of propagation accuracy and the consistency of aGNSS availability are performed with real GNSS data acquired from a LEO satellite in orbit. Major functionalities are presented for further exploration of a snapshot GNSS system customizable to the needs of a variety of LEO satellites, with a focus on CubeSat class missions.

items.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
items.abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.

items.title: Augmented Brand Intelligence in Marketing: How Human-AI Complementarity Shapes Consumer-Brand Interactions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing and consumer-brand interactions through personalization, efficiency, prediction, and scalability. Its expanding role, however, raises a more fundamental question: what does AI add to consumer interactions, and where does human involvement remain especially valuable? Using signaling theory as its principal explanatory lens, this chapter develops the concept of augmented brand intelligence to explain how human and artificial intelligence can function as complementary sources of brand signals in consumer-facing interactions. A structured critical synthesis of research on AI in marketing, human-AI collaboration, consumer responses to AI, signaling, and consumer-brand relationships suggests that human involvement can signal relational capability through empathy, contextual judgment, relational understanding, and authentic engagement, whereas AI can signal technological capability through efficiency, personalization, analytical capability, and innovation. The framework distinguishes signal complementarity from signal congruence: complementarity concerns whether human and AI signals contribute distinct, nonredundant information about the brand or the capabilities it offers, whereas congruence concerns whether those signals convey compatible meanings about the brand. Complementary signals are expected to reduce perceived information asymmetry more strongly when congruence is high, because consumers can integrate distinct information into a coherent interpretation of the brand. The framework is illustrated across five application domains: customer service, personalization, brand communication, recommendation systems, and customer relationship management. By moving beyond a substitution-focused perspective, the chapter explains how the orchestration of human and AI capabilities can create credible, trusted, and relationally meaningful consumer experiences, and concludes with managerial guidance and an agenda for empirical research across diverse consumer, brand, and technological contexts.

items.title: Autonomous AI Agents for Software Development: From Code Generation to Automated Testing
items.abstract: This research paper presents a proposed framework for Autonomous AI Agents for Software Development, focusing on the transition from code generation to automated testing, debugging, and software verification. The paper introduces a modular, role-based architecture consisting of a planner agent, context retriever, coder agent, tester agent, debugger agent, and reviewer agent. These components work together through a bounded Plan-Code-Test-Repair workflow to understand software requirements, retrieve relevant code, generate changes, execute tests, diagnose failures, and improve code quality. The proposed framework emphasizes functional correctness, automated test generation, repository-level issue resolution, secure tool execution, human approval, and auditability. It also outlines an evaluation protocol using established benchmarks and metrics to assess code correctness, test quality, efficiency, cost, reliability, and security. This work synthesizes existing research on large language models, reasoning-and-acting agents, self-debugging, multi-agent systems, and automated software testing. It provides a conceptual architecture and evaluation plan for future implementation and experimentation. No implemented system or benchmark results are claimed in this paper. The research aims to support the development of more reliable, secure, and transparent AI-assisted software engineering systems.

items.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
items.abstract: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.

items.title: Balancing Support and Mobility: Multimodal Evaluation of Exoskeleton in Live Veterinary Surgeries
items.abstract: Passive neck-support exoskeletons may reduce surgical physical workload, but conventional summaries of the entire task may not catch when these benefits emerge and how muscle activity and posture evolve together. This study evaluated a passive neck-support exoskeleton during 36 live veterinary surgeries performed by 10 surgeons using EMG and IMU measures. Statistical analyses included linear mixed models for task-average EMG and IMU outcomes, generalized additive mixed models for time-varying intervention effects, and lagged cross-correlation analyses for EMG-IMU temporal coupling. The exoskeleton significantly reduced the neck range of motion. Temporal analyses showed delayed reductions in upper trapezius activation, with decreases during the middle-to-late phase of surgery, and direction-specific changes in head-neck kinematics. Coupling analysis showed stronger %MVE-posture coupling in the control condition, but stronger MPF-posture coupling under intervention. These findings suggest that passive neck support may reduce muscle loading and alter fatigue-related muscle-posture coordination during prolonged surgical work.

items.title: Behavioral Intention Towards Artificial Intelligence Integration and Teachers’ Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has reshaped instructional practices, making teachers’ readiness and confidence critical considerations. This study determined the level of Grade 7 teachers’ behavioral intention towards AI integration and self-efficacy. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of age, sex, position, educational attainment, and AI-related training; their behavioral intention based on attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control; their self-efficacy concerning student engagement, instructional strategy, and classroom management; the relationship between the two variables; and whether respondents’ profile moderates this relationship. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 185 Grade 7 teachers from the districts of Kadingilan, Damulog, Kibawe, and Dangcagan in the Division of Bukidnon, selected through universal sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made questionnaire. Mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for statistical treatment. Findings revealed a very high level of behavioral intention and self-efficacy among teachers, with a significant positive relationship between the two variables, further moderated by respondents’ profile, particularly position and trainings attended. The study concludes that teachers’ favorable behavioral intention toward AI strengthens their self-efficacy. It is recommended that school heads may enhance teachers’ readiness and confidence in integrating AI into instruction.

items.title: Beyond Forecast Accuracy: A Responsible AI Framework for Provenance-Aware Fine Jewelry Retail Planning
items.abstract: Fine jewelry retailers must reconcile uncertain demand, high-value inventory, complex material histories, and expectations of responsible sourcing. This article develops a responsible artificial intelligence framework that connects demand forecasting, provenance evidence, and governance within retail planning. A conceptual framework-development approach informed by design-science research combines a targeted literature update through October 9, 2026, with descriptive analysis of published market statistics and an external retail forecasting benchmark. The analysis distinguishes original design propositions from empirical findings reported by other researchers; no retailer-level experiment or environmental impact assessment was conducted. Three sourced bar charts illustrate changing gold jewelry consumption and the methodological relevance of inventory-based model evaluation. The resulting architecture integrates data inputs, predictive analytics, provenance and traceability, ethical governance, and human-reviewed decisions with feedback. Five design principles and five testable propositions specify how forecasts can inform assortment, replenishment, allocation, and sourcing while preserving evidence quality and accountability. The framework shifts evaluation from forecast accuracy alone toward decision quality under explicit operational and provenance constraints. It also separates inventory efficiency, sourcing documentation, and environmental outcomes, preventing improvements in one category from being misrepresented as proof of another. Managerial implications include staged implementation, evidence-qualified sourcing rules, meaningful review authority, and documented overrides. Future validation should compare complete decision policies, preserve temporal information boundaries, measure calibrated reliance, and assess environmental consequences independently. The article contributes a sector-specific architecture and evaluation agenda for accountable retail intelligence without claiming that the integrated framework has already demonstrated operational or sustainability benefits across fine jewelry businesses and markets.

items.title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
items.abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.

items.title: Blinded professional ratings of artificial intelligence–generated and dietitian-designed meal plans
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence-assisted systems increasingly produce personalized meal plans, but their value depends on whether clinicians judge those plans credible and usable. We evaluated complete plans from a constrained artificial intelligence-assisted pipeline under blinded professional review. METHODS: In a cross-sectional exploratory web study, 54 eligible anonymous evaluator records from Brazilian dietitians contributed 130 evaluations of five matched plan pairs, with one pipeline-generated and one dietitian-designed plan per persona. Evaluators rated nine items across three domains and were offered an optional pairwise plan preference task. The overall score required all nine items and was available for 124 evaluations. RESULTS: Pipeline-generated plans received a mean rating of 3.67 (standard deviation, 0.57) (n = 59) compared with 3.11 (standard deviation, 0.73) for comparator plans (n = 65) (d = 0.86). Among 38 evaluator records with complete scores for both origins, 31 favored pipeline-generated plans, 6 favored dietitian-designed plans, and 1 had equal mean scores for both origins (paired t[37] = 5.32, P < 0.001). Pipeline-generated plans received higher ratings in all five persona pairs. This pattern was descriptive because evaluator records overlapped across pairs. Domain differences were +0.76 for nutritional adequacy, +0.69 for technical quality, and +0.21 for practical applicability. In the optional task, 32 of 42 eligible pairwise choices selected the pipeline-generated plan as more appropriate. CONCLUSIONS: Under blinded presentation, practicing dietitians gave plans from the constrained pipeline a mean rating above the neutral anchor of the 5-point scale. These findings support prospective evaluation of a structured first draft workflow, with required clinician edits and patient-relevant outcomes as endpoints.

items.title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
items.abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.

items.title: Building creative momentum: Social and psychological factors associated with flow in Chinese artists.
items.abstract: Flow is a deeply immersive psychological state characterized by intense concentration, intrinsic motivation, and a perceived balance between challenge and skill. Although prior research has examined flow in contexts such as sports, education, and workplace performance, limited attention has been paid to how social, cognitive, and motivational factors are associated with flow experiences among practicing artists. This study examined the relationships among perceived social support, the positive mindset dimension, creative process, expected self/life, and flow among practicing artists in China. Drawing on a sample of 962 artists, the study employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to assess theoretically informed associations among social support from friends, family, and significant others, internal psychological factors, and flow experiences. The findings showed that creative process and expected self/life were positively associated with flow-related experiences, whereas the positive mindset dimension was not directly associated with flow. Social support was also associated with internal psychological factors relevant to creative engagement. Mediation analyses indicated that creative process and expected self/life were significant indirect pathways linking the positive mindset dimension and flow. The model demonstrated satisfactory explanatory and predictive relevance, supporting the integration of social and psychological correlates in understanding flow among artistic populations. These findings highlight the relevance of supportive social environments and internal psychological resources in relation to creative engagement and flow, while acknowledging that the cross-sectional and self-report design does not permit causal or temporal conclusions.

items.title: Can AI agents make law? Evaluating AI legal relevance and creativity
items.abstract: Large language models, the artificial intelligence (AI) systems behind modern chatbots, are trained on vast amounts of legal text, but can they build on it to write law for situations that text never anticipated? In this study, we analyse AI agents' ability to draft a hypothetical "Constitution" for a "community of AI agents". We design "constitutional assemblies" in which a single language model plays several characters that debate to produce a draft constitution. We find that the assemblies converge on a robust floor of legal provisions, and generate a wide variety of different proposals around it, including several AI-specific provisions with no equivalent in human law. Looking more closely at the "creativity" of these AI agents, we find different levels: most proposals combine existing concepts and themes from human constitutions with AI-specific vocabulary. We introduce a measure of this recombination, which helps identify and highlight the most novel legal material. This study reveals a ceiling on AI creativity: the agents extend familiar legal ideas to new situations, but they do not work through what those situations would change. Although current AI models can help develop new laws, they still depend on human legal reasoning.

items.title: Can AI Assistants Trigger Mental Illness in Users?
items.abstract: As conversational artificial intelligence models become ubiquitous fixtures in professional and personal workflows, the nature of human-tool interaction has the potential to gradually shift from mechanical utility to parasocial dependency. While existing literature frequently addresses adverse events related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual deskilling, the pathopsychological sequelae of sustained AI integration remain largely unexamined. Here, we describe and preliminarily characterize the AI Assistant Syndrome, a human psychiatric construct encompassing acute chatbot-induced anxiety and mental exhaustion. This preliminary description will guide future systematic investigations to recognize, prevent, and treat this syndrome.

items.title: Can LLM Agents Resolve Service Failures? Simulating Multi-Turn Complaint Handling under Information Asymmetry
items.abstract: LLM agents are widely adopted in service chatbots for rule-guided support and information access, yet emotionally demanding complaint handling still relies heavily on human agents. We introduce ServiceBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to complaint handling, with 2,500 scenarios spanning 184 complaint categories and five service industries. We propose Asymmetric Progressive Complaint Simulation (APCS) to simulate realistic complaint handling, together with a justice-based evaluation framework. Our experiments reveal that even capable LLM agents struggle to handle complaints effectively. They lack the ability to proactively gather information and strategically guide conversations toward resolution, often resorting to premature compensation. We further show that targeted post-training with SFT and DPO substantially improves these capabilities, enabling a smaller model to match or surpass much larger models on several outcomes.

items.title: Causal reasoning subgraph retrieval for coal mine safety risk assessment
items.abstract: Coal mine safety risk assessment can reduce accidents, but traditional methods rely on subjective expert judgment or isolated sensor monitoring, which cannot assess complex and interrelated diverse security risks. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework based on causal reasoning knowledge subgraphs. We first construct a coal mine safety knowledge graph that integrates risk factors, solutions, and legal bases by employing a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers with whole word masking combined with Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory and Conditional Random Field (BERT‑wwm‑BiLSTM‑CRF) for entity recognition and BERT-wwm-BiLSTM-Attention for relation extraction. Then we retrieve a causal reasoning subgraph from this graph through relation expansion, node screening, and semantic pruning. This subgraph is provided to the large language model (LLM) to make risk assessment. Experimental results show an accuracy of 95.9%.

items.title: Christian Higher Education: Biblical Foundations, Curriculum Integrity, Digital Learning, and Quality Assurance
items.abstract: Christian higher education is simultaneously a confessional undertaking, an educational institution and, where it awards recognised qualifications, a subject of public academic accountability. Treating any one identity as sufficient weakens both institutional witness and learner protection. This chapter develops a biblically grounded, academically rigorous and context-sensitive account of quality governance for Christian universities, theological seminaries, ministry-training providers and faith-based programmes. A purposive critical synthesis of Scripture, historical and contemporary theological-education scholarship, curriculum and assessment theory, selected theological-education standards, and Rwandan regulatory instruments distinguishes theological commitments from empirically assessable educational claims and binding legal duties. It examines Sola Scriptura, hermeneutical competence, professional curriculum integration, doctrinal accountability, online formation, artificial intelligence, research ethics, governance, accreditation and transnational delivery. The central proposition is that mission fidelity does not substitute for educational effectiveness, and neither establishes legal recognition; instead, all three require distinct evidence and appropriate decision authority. The chapter advances a proposed Christian Higher Education Curriculum and Quality Assurance Framework situated within Integrated Evidence-Traceable Quality Governance and operationalised through a mission-alignment matrix, programme-design criteria, digital discipleship rubric, institutional self-assessment and worked hypothetical review. These instruments are neither regulator-approved nor empirically validated. The resulting approach treats faithful biblical teaching, scholarly competence, responsible stewardship and truthful public representation as mutually reinforcing obligations without confusing scriptural authority with the methods of empirical investigation or the powers of statutory regulators.

items.title: Clinical validation of artificial intelligence for cancer detection prognosis and analysis across imaging modalities and tumor types
items.abstract: This study evaluates the diagnostic and prognostic performance of artificial intelligence in cancer detection across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review synthesizes current evidence on deep learning, radiomics, multimodal integration, and precision oncology frameworks, with emphasis on validation quality and clinical translation. A systematic review of 180 peer reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted. Included investigations assessed artificial intelligence applications in radiology, digital pathology, endoscopy, PET imaging, and multimodal platforms. Extracted data covered diagnostic accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, dataset size, validation strategy, and study design. Subdomains included detection, prognosis, grading, survival prediction, radio-genomics, explainability, federated learning, and regulatory evaluation. Across breast, lung, prostate, colorectal, brain, and skin cancers, multiple high-quality cohorts reported AUC values above 0.90. Whole slide histopathology achieved the highest discrimination, reaching AUC 0.99 in curated datasets. CT and MRI systems demonstrated strong performance with multicenter validation, including large scale lung and breast screening studies. Radiomics contributed to survival prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, and molecular subtype inference. Multimodal and transformer-based architectures improved representation learning in volumetric and cross domain data. Despite strong retrospective performance, only 21 percent of studies included external validation, 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets, and 6 percent applied prospective or temporal validation. Artificial intelligence shows consistent high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging domains. Strongest evidence supports adjunctive use in screening, digital pathology, and endoscopic detection. Broader clinical adoption requires prospective trials, multicenter external validation, standardized reporting, explainability integration, and alignment with regulatory frameworks to ensure reliable deployment in precision oncology.

items.title: Closing the Gap: An Action Research Study on Synchronizing EnglishLanguage and Computing Skills Curricula in an Omani General Foundation Program
items.abstract: Historically, General Foundation Programs (GFPs) in Oman have delivered Foundation English Language Learning (FEL) and Foundation Computing Skills (FCS) as parallel but non-communicating courses. The June 2025 revision of the Oman Core Academic Learning Outcomes (OCALOs) addresses this separation by mandating an integrated Fundamental Academic Skills (FAS) component. Unlike broader integration models such as CLIL or standalone PBL, this study synchronizes the timing of FCS instruction with the immediate requirements of FEL academic tasks, ensuring computing instruction directly serves academic output requirements. This action research study responds to that mandate by designing, piloting, and evaluating a synchronized curricular model at the School of Foundation Studies (SoFS), National University of Science and Technology (NU). Using a two-cycle action research design, the study audited existing FEL and FCS syllabi, developed a synchronized delivery plan, and piloted the model across two foundation levels totaling 79 students. Data was triangulated across student artifacts, survey responses, and faculty meeting records to evaluate skill transfer, task coherence, and student reliance on generative AI tools. The study confirmed measurable skill transfer, improved task coherence, and reduced student reliance on generative AI tools through synchronized delivery and shared assessment criteria. The key finding is that shared marking criteria between FEL and FCS faculty, rather than curriculum redesign alone, is the essential bridge that makes skill transfer successful in practice. This study offers a structural roadmap for Omani HEIs to operationalize the FAS mandate under the revised OAAAQA standards.

items.title: Cognitive Engagement, Learning Strategies, Adjustment to College and Academic Motivation: A Structural Equation Model on Academic Success Among College Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Two Approaches for Improved Site Safety: Domain Approach versus General End-to-End Compliance Reasoning
items.abstract: Abstract Field compliance checking seeks to automate the process of extracting safety requirements, capturing site information, identifying violations, and generating documentation for different responsible parties to improve construction site safety. However, existing safety checking methods are typically limited in their ability to employ domain knowledge and multimodal data, and they often lack generalizability and scalability. There is also limited effort to automatically generate natural-language descriptions of compliance-checking results for documentation purposes. Aimed toward addressing these gaps, this paper studies and compares two approaches for automated safety checking: a domain approach and an end-to-end approach. The domain approach integrates existing domain-specific information extraction, site visual information detection, and knowledge graph–based compliance reasoning methods. The end-to-end approach relies on multimodal foundation models. The comparative analysis evaluates the information extraction and compliance reasoning capabilities of both approaches in terms of performance, errors, and limitations. The results showed that the domain approach achieved strong performance with good potential for generalizability and adaptability. In contrast, the end-to-end approach requires additional fine-tuning to achieve comparable results.

items.title: Competitive Intelligence in the Age of Digital Transformation: Challenges and Opportunities: A Nigerian Perspective
items.abstract: This study analyses the impact of digital tools such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data on the activities of Nigerian companies. This process is called Competitive Intelligence (CI). The study also finds that though these tools offer great opportunities, there is an “Intelligence Paradox” in Nigeria. It indicates that firms have a lot of data at hand but tend to grapple with leveraging it into proper business advice. This is largely caused by bad infrastructure like poor power supply and expensive internet, plus new privacy laws, including the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023. To tackle these problems, the research recommends low-cost methods such as Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) the use of free, public information, while ensuring humans are in charge of machines’ work. To succeed in business in Nigeria, Nigerian firms must develop their own "Compliant Intelligence" using smart technologies that are compliant with the law, the paper concludes. Mixing global technology with local knowledge helps businesses stay ahead in a tough economy.

items.title: Comprehensive Analytical Study on Spatial Reasoning and Adaptation of Human Brain Versus Artificial Intelligence - A Review Report
items.abstract: Recent advances in computer vision, spatial computing, robotics, and embodied artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved machine capabilities in visual perception, navigation, spatial reasoning, and object manipulation. However, performance on structured benchmarks and controlled environments does not necessarily demonstrate equivalence to human spatial intelligence in complex real-world situations. This review examines whether current AI systems can reproduce the breadth and flexibility of human spatial and embodied intelligence, with particular emphasis on their implications for the potential replacement of humans by AI. The review synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature on human spatial cognition, embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robotics, and relevant AI capability benchmarks. The evidence is organised around four dimensions: (1) biological sensorimotor coupling and proprioception, (2) zero-shot spatial problem-solving and dynamic affordance recognition, (3) physical common-sense reasoning and adaptation, and (4) energy-efficient and context-sensitive spatial processing. Existing research indicates that AI systems have achieved considerable progress in perception, navigation, planning, and manipulation, but continue to encounter challenges involving unfamiliar environments, occlusion, uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, changing object configurations, physical interaction, long-horizon adaptation, and generalisation beyond training distributions. Human spatial intelligence, in contrast, integrates perception, proprioception, embodied experience, contextual knowledge, physical intuition, memory, and flexible real-time decision-making as an interconnected system. The reviewed evidence therefore suggests that current AI can augment and extend human spatial capabilities but cannot yet reproduce the breadth, adaptability, embodied experience, and contextual flexibility of human spatial intelligence. Spatial ability consequently represents an important dimension of human irreplaceability and supports a future paradigm of human–AI complementarity rather than complete human substitution.

items.title: Conceptualising AI-reform professional learning communities in Chinese schools through the lion dance metaphor
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves into school education at increasing speed, we still know relatively little about how schools organise AI-related change amid policy expectations, technological uncertainty and teachers’ everyday work. Based on a qualitative case study of an AI education pilot school in Beijing, China, this article examines the formation and operation of an AI-reform professional learning community (PLC). Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, school-based observations and school documents. Through inductive thematic analysis, four recurring role functions were identified and subsequently conceptualised through the structural metaphor of the Chinese lion dance: drummers, lion heads, lion tails and audiences. The findings show that school leaders translated policy expectations and paced implementation; teacher leaders carried visible exploratory and pedagogical work; non-lead teachers extended reform through cautious and selective participation; and parents, while remaining outside the formal community, shaped ethical boundaries and conditions of trust. The article conceptualises AI-reform PLCs as issue-specific and role-differentiated communities that organise policy translation, teacher learning, leadership, participation and ethical negotiation around emerging technological change. It contributes a culturally grounded account of how school-based AI reform is collectively coordinated rather than simply implemented by individual teachers.

items.title: ConCI: A Controlled Counterfactual Benchmark for Contextual Integrity in LLMs
items.abstract: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that the appropriateness of sharing personal information depends on the context of the information flow, not on the information alone. However, existing CI benchmarks often use independent scenarios that vary multiple CI parameters simultaneously and are dominated by inappropriate flows, making it unclear whether correct predictions reflect sensitivity to context or a general refusal tendency. We present ConCI, a controlled-counterfactual benchmark in which an anchor flow is paired with two counterfactuals that each modify a single CI parameter. The resulting triplet is scored jointly, with credit given only when all three flows are judged correctly. Built from six existing benchmarks, ConCI contains 1,592 flows in 556 triplets, is approximately label-balanced, and is validated by seven human annotators per flow. Across seven LLMs, many correct anchor predictions fail on at least one counterfactual, and even the strongest model errs on about a fifth of triplets. Furthermore, models perform near ceiling on inappropriate flows but weaker on appropriate ones, often continuing to judge a flow inappropriate even when a contextual change should make it appropriate. Larger models narrow this bias toward non-disclosure but do not eliminate it, and reasoning yields only modest gains.

items.title: Current applications of artificial intelligence for advancing agriculture, sustainability and climate mitigation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.

items.title: Data Sovereignty, Stewardship, and Generative AI in Oral History: A Discussion Paper from the International Digital Oral History Lab
items.abstract: This working paper is issued by the International Digital Oral History Lab (https://idohl.org/) as part of its ongoing work on the responsible use of generative AI in oral history. It brings together evidence from oral history practice, AI governance, technical infrastructure, commercial and open source platforms, professional guidance and scholarship. It examines questions of informed consent, confidentiality, shared authority, data and participant sovereignty, and the responsibilities of those who steward oral history interviews. The paper argues that data sovereignty in oral history encompasses more than storage location, privacy or legal compliance. It also concerns who controls interviews, who participates in decisions about their use, and how obligations to interviewees can be maintained within rapidly changing technological environments. This is a discussion paper rather than a definitive policy statement or a systematic review. It documents the Lab’s emerging understanding, identifies tensions and uncertainties, and contributes to discussion about responsible stewardship in an AI-mediated future. Version 1, dated 17 October 2026, was developed by the contributing authors named in the document. The International Digital Oral History Lab maintains the document and coordinates future revisions. Authorship of subsequent versions will be recorded separately.

items.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
items.abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.

items.title: Defining AGI: Solution/Abundance/Apocalypse/God
items.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) has changed from a scientific aim to a moving goalpost of industrial AI ambitions. As far as the AI industry is concerned, it is simultaneously the most consequential invention in human history and a manageable, iterative technology. But what is AGI, aside from a future promise? This paper identifies four rhetorical registers through which AGI is defined, in the words of those giving it shape. In doing so, we base ourselves on the AI industry’s own discussions of AGI, including the 2026 India AI Impact Summit, AI companies’ blog posts, and journalistic coverage. Taken together, these source materials are treated as institutionalized performances of a collectively held sociotechnical imaginary through which AGI is stabilized and reproduced. As such, AGI is positioned as the next supposedly inevitable threshold on the road to superintelligence, imbued with the promise to solve all problems (a techno-solutionist register), bring prosperity (techno-utopian), pose an existential threat to humanity (techno-apocalyptic), and become no less than god (techno-theological). These rhetorical registers together capture AGI as an ineluctable sociotechnical imaginary, as it is being spoken into existence.

items.title: Deployment of edge-lightweight AI vertical models in multimodal anomaly detection and energy optimization of tech-long production line
items.abstract: Aiming at the problems that the abnormal state of high-speed liquid packaging production lines is difficult to identify in time, the computing power of edge controller is limited, and the energy consumption regulation and condition monitoring are separated from each other, a multimodal lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) system embedded in Tech-Long production controller is constructed; this realizes the collaborative optimization of abnormal operation window identification and energy consumption of the whole line. First, this study collects vibration, acoustic, and thermal signals from the bottle blowing, filling, and packaging sections; it also constructs cross-sectional anomaly characterization through time synchronization, feature-level alignment, and hierarchical fusion. Subsequently, Feather Convolutional Neural Network (FeatherCNN) is reconstructed using kernel fusion, channel compression, and 4-bit Integer (INT4) quantization to reduce model computation and storage load; thus, the network can adapt to resource-constrained Advanced RISC Machine (ARM) edge controllers. Finally, a dual-layer control chain is built, composed of continuous basic energy-saving and anomaly risk-weighted correction, so that anomaly scores influence the updates of temperature zones, valve openings, and heat-sealing parameters via dynamic weights and adjustment gains. The experimental results demonstrate that the anomaly window recognition accuracy of multimodal FeatherCNN reaches 0.931, which is superior to traditional machine learning models, deep learning baselines and various single-modal structures. The lightweight processing reduces Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) from 3.42×10⁹ to 0.58×10⁹, a decrease of approximately 83%. The inference latency of the complete model on the ARM controller is shortened from 18.63 milliseconds (ms) to 7.41 ms. Under the controlled conditions of fixed production line speed, material specifications, and statistical windows, the dual-layer collaborative control has reduced the overall energy consumption of the whole line by 26%. The results show that multimodal anomaly identification, model lightweighting, and energy-saving parameter tuning can work together in the same edge decision chain. The framework verifies the feasibility of resource-constrained controllers supporting abnormal monitoring and energy consumption regulation of the entire packaging line; meanwhile, it provides an engineering reference for edge intelligent deployment of similar high-speed liquid packaging lines.

items.title: Designing the Decision Supply Chain: A Framework for Human-AI Complementarity in Organizations
items.abstract: Organizations are rapidly expanding their capacity to generate and process information through data, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet greater intelligence does not necessarily translate into coordinated organizational action. As AI increasingly participates in organizational decision-making, a central managerial challenge is shifting from generating information to designing systems that transform distributed intelligence into effective decisions, coordinated action, and organizational learning. This chapter introduces Decision Supply Chain, defined as the interconnected organizational system through which signals are sensed, information is interpreted, alternatives are generated and evaluated, decisions are authorized, actions are executed, and outcomes inform subsequent decisions. The concept shifts the unit of analysis from individual decisions toward the architecture and coordination of interdependent decision activities across actors, technologies, and organizational boundaries. Although represented as a chain, the Decision Supply Chain is conceptualized as a networked and recursive system incorporating feedback, interdependence, and learning. Drawing on bounded rationality (Simon, 1957), tacit knowledge (Polanyi, 1966), Organizational Information Processing Theory (Galbraith, 1974), and research on human-AI collaboration, delegation, complementarity, and task allocation (Fügener et al., 2022, 2026; Puranam, 2021; Shrestha et al., 2019), the chapter develops a framework for Decision Supply Chain Design. It proposes that the allocation, coordination, and governance of human and AI decision activities should vary according to five characteristics of the decision context: uncertainty, consequence, reversibility, frequency, and interdependence. The framework further identifies risks arising from inappropriate human-AI configurations, including misaligned optimization, erosion of tacit knowledge, diminished human agency, and weakened organizational learning. The chapter argues that advantage from AI may depend not only on superior algorithms or information-processing capacity but increasingly on an organization's ability to orchestrate complementary human and AI capabilities across interconnected decision processes. Decision Supply Chain Design therefore offers a systems-level perspective for understanding how organizations can convert AI-enabled intelligence into coordinated action and sustained organizational learning.
